f: A Smithsonian museum. The Smithsonian gets roughly 60% of its money from the federal government, the rest from private gifts and earned income.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment.

f: The art museum of Indiana University, a public state university.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment.

n: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts
f: David Koch, of Koch Industries, paid to modernise the New York State Theater, which now carries his name as the David H. Koch Theater.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels.

A New Yorker profile that Sidney Blumenthal forwarded to Hillary Clinton says David Koch gave $100 million in 2008 to modernise Lincoln Center's New York State Theatre, which now bears his name. It says the Kochs operate oil refineries and pipelines. (news item forwarded in a leak)

f: A Ukrainian city museum until 2022. Under Russian occupation it is run by the culture ministry of the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, which the US, EU and UK list as a sanctioned entity.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Its Kuindzhi paintings were taken to a museum in Donetsk after the city fell in 2022.
x: Bellingcat, 2022-06-07

Bellingcat found the Kuindzhi Museum damaged but standing, with a sign placing it under the Donetsk People's Republic culture ministry. Mayor's adviser Petro Andryushchenko said its Kuindzhi paintings were handed to occupiers. The Moscow Times traced them to a Donetsk museum.

f: Rebuilt by Russian authorities and reopened on 28 December 2025 under the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, which the US, EU and UK list as a sanctioned entity.
w: Flags: Sanctions. A Russian airstrike hit it on 16 March 2022 while civilians sheltered inside; AP counted close to 600 dead.
x: Bellingcat, 2025-11-14

Bellingcat's report on Russia rebuilding Mariupol recalls the 16 March 2022 airstrike on the drama theatre where civilians sheltered; AP counted close to 600 dead. Russian authorities reopened the rebuilt theatre on 28 December 2025, with St Petersburg's governor present.

f: Private centre founded in 2006 and run by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation. Pinchuk's fortune comes from Interpipe, a maker of steel pipes and railway wheels. No corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2020 two prize nominees withdrew with open letters after 28 guides were dismissed. The centre denies the sackings were over their union.

n: Bienal de Artes Mediales de Santiago
f: Chile's Ministry of Cultures, through its collaborating-organisations programme and audiovisual fund, plus donations under the Cultural Donations Law. 2025 partners: SURA, Nescafé, La Tercera, Radio 13c.
w: Run since 1993 by the Corporación Chilena de Video y Artes Electrónicas. The 17th edition ran 9 to 26 October 2025, centred on the GAM.

f: Limited company owned by art collectors including Samit Gehlot (Intex Foundation), Tony Wainaina and Robert Devereux. It sells at international fairs and runs an annual East African art auction.
w: Founded in 2012 under director Danda Jaroljmek. Built its first white-cube gallery in 2015 and joined Cromwell Place, London, in 2020.

n: Colección de Arte Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat
f: Private museum run by the Fundación Amalia Lacroze de Fortabat, set up by the Loma Negra cement heiress. No sponsor list, budget or donor list is published.
w: Opened in October 2008 in a Rafael Viñoly building in Puerto Madero. The foundation also runs the Premio Fortabat art prize.

f: Uruguayan state museum, a division of the Dirección Nacional de Cultura in the Ministry of Education and Culture. No sponsor list is published.
w: Created by law in 1911 as the Museo de Bellas Artes. Holds more than 7,000 works, mostly by Uruguayan artists.

f: Commercial gallery founded in 2016 by British Lebanese construction owner Marwan Zakhem. Its Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize pays GHC 50,000 to the winner. No sponsors or financing details are listed.
w: Spaces in Accra and London. Runs the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize for Ghanaian women artists. No source names the founder's company.

f: Non-profit platform founded in 2010 in Donetsk. The EU's Creative Europe programme co-funds its ZMINA project with Trans Europe Halles and Malý Berlín. No current donor list is published.
w: Russian-backed forces seized its Donetsk site in June 2014 and run a prison there. The foundation moved to Kyiv.

f: Founded 1996 as Ukraine's first gallery with municipal status. The city council culture department decides on its premises. No budget, sponsor list or donor list is published.
w: Upper halls closed since 2022; the ARTbasement, also a shelter, reopened in September 2023. In March 2023 the mayor said the premises stay a gallery.

f: Edo State Government, Germany's Foreign Office, Mellon Foundation, British Museum and PI Trust are founding partners. Leadership Circle donors include NNPC, Seplat Energy, Lekoil and Azura Power.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. Edo's governor said on 7 November 2025 it would become the Benin Royal Museum. Oba loyalists disrupted the 9 November preview. Open by appointment only.

f: State enterprise. 2025: UAH 38.0M state budget, UAH 24.2M own income. Project partners include Erste Foundation, British Council, the US Embassy and International Renaissance Foundation.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, State censorship or punishment. In July 2013 the then-director had a mural painted black and a painting pulled; artists called a boycott. 2025 visitors: 53,870.

f: State museum. The Cabinet gave it UAH 5.6M in 2020 for emergency facade repairs. Donations go to its own charitable foundation. No corporate sponsor list is published.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In October 2012 staff sent an open letter and protested against acting director Tatiana Mironova, named after the Ministry of Culture removed Anatoliy Melnyk.

f: Private foundation set up by Eduardo Costantini covers the annual deficit; own income pays about half the budget. Corporate partners: Consultatio, ICBC, Bloomberg, Alcorta.
w: Costantini's ex-wife Teresa said in August 2026 she will go to court over works in the founding collection; MALBA says its foundation owns them.

n: Museo de la Solidaridad Salvador Allende
f: Servicio Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural grant of CLP 660M in 2025. Project money from Fondart, the Senate, Henry Moore Foundation and Centro Cultural de España. Metro is a media partner.
w: In 2023 pressure from Allende's grandson over Tania Bruguera's show delayed its opening; it opened in modified form. In-person visitors in 2025: 10,337.

n: Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico
f: Private nonprofit. Current exhibitions are backed by the Flamboyan Foundation, Mellon Foundation, Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, Mano Amiga and the Puerto Rico Tourism Company. Members and corporate donors also give.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In November 2023 activists protested after a gallery named for Cecilia Orta Allende was renamed for a donor family tied to the Fiscal Control Board.

f: National Museums of Kenya, a state corporation, runs it. Planet Africa (2024 to 2025) was funded by the German Research Foundation and Germany's Foreign Office. No sponsor list is published.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In May 2017 museum management banned works by Michael Soi, Patrick Mukabi and Bertiers Mbatia as unsuitable for children, days before opening.

n: National Museum of Fine Arts of Chile (MNBA)
f: State museum; the Servicio Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural pays for acquisitions. Recent gifts came through Fundación AMA from collector Juan Yarur Torres, and from artist Cecilia Vicuña.
w: Record 510,720 visitors in 2024. Cancelled a León Ferrari retrospective in June 2026, citing budget cuts. Not the Buenos Aires museum of that name.

f: Run by the Fundación Municipal Bienal de Cuenca, a city body. The 17th edition cost about $1.2M, from municipal money, private-company agreements and self-raised funds. No sponsors are named.
w: Founded in 1986 as a painting biennial. In November 2025 it reported threats over one work, filed a complaint and kept it on view.

f: Founded by musician X Alfonso. In 2014 the Cuban Music Institute and Ministry of Culture were covering some costs until it became self-financing. No current sponsor list is published.
w: Opened in a former cooking-oil factory in 2014. Announced a temporary closure in June 2026, which state agency Prensa Latina ties to the US embargo.

f: Organised by Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta, a state-funded foundation created in 2010. The Yogyakarta regional government ran the 2019 edition. No corporate sponsors found.
w: On 9 October 2026 the foundation announced it is closing after 16 years, citing rising censorship and violence against activists in Indonesia.

f: Run since 2024 by Majelis Jakarta, a network of artist collectives. 2026 partners: Dulux, Artotel's Paviliun Raden Saleh hotel and internet provider iForte. Main budget and public grants are unpublished.
w: Founded 1974 by the Jakarta Arts Council. The 2026 edition, KEBAL, runs 4 Oct to 28 Nov at Taman Ismail Marzuki.

f: Run privately by Ayala Foundation, the Ayala group's foundation. Ayala Corporation co-presents shows; BPI is a partner. The Spanish and US embassies backed the 2024 to 2025 Zobel show.
w: Opened 1967 from Fernando Zobel's plan. It closed in 2019 for rebuilding and reopened 4 December 2021. It had 65,000 visitors in 2014.

f: Private museum founded in 2010 to show the collection of physician and patron Dr. Joven Cuanang. Run by the non-profit Silangan Foundation; entry is ticketed. No corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Housed in a complex by artist Antonio Leaño inside a two-hectare botanical garden. The collection centres on Salingpusa and other Filipino contemporary artists.

f: Privately owned by DTAC telecom founder Boonchai Bencharongkul, who built it in 2012 for his collection of over 1,000 works. His son Kanachai runs it; tickets cost THB 250.
w: Also runs a Four Seasons art space and a Suvarnabhumi airport display. No sponsors or public grants are listed.

f: Part of PETRONAS, Malaysia's state oil and gas company, which has built the PETRONAS Art Collection since 1993. Nearly two million visitors since 1992.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Left Suria KLCC at the end of July 2026. A preview opened at Ombak KLCC on 21 August; full opening is due by end 2027.

f: Administrative corporation. 2025 revenue NT$201M: Tainan City subsidy NT$89.7M, Ministry of Culture and others NT$25M, tickets and parking NT$57M, donations NT$3.7M.
w: Opened 27 January 2019. In 2025 the Ministry of Culture set up a preparatory office for a planned Tainan National Art Museum.

f: Private museum built by collectors Yan Shijie and Cao Mei, who invested nearly RMB 400 million over eight years. It opened in 2014 and sells memberships; no sponsors are listed.
w: The 20,000 sq m site was designed by Dong Yugan of Peking University. Its founder is described only as a collector and entrepreneur.

f: Non-profit artist-initiated space founded in 2007 with the Vietnam Foundation for the Arts. In 2014 it reported no domestic public funding and relied on international donors and a benefit auction.
w: Vietnam's Cultural Police forced cancellations and a warning in 2016; the state does not fund it, so that is a note. In 2016 it closed its residency studio indefinitely after three cancelled exhibitions and a Cultural Po

f: Run by the collectives ruangrupa, Serrum and Grafis Huru Hara. Its own income covers about 30 percent of costs; their businesses pay the rest. It sought local funds in 2022.
w: Name to know: co-founder ruangrupa curated documenta fifteen in 2022, which drew antisemitism accusations; it apologised for stereotypes in one mural.

f: State gallery owned by Indonesia's Culture Ministry, a ministry created under President Prabowo; before that it sat under the education and culture ministry. Holds 1,770 artworks.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. On 19 December 2024 it cancelled Yos Suprapto's solo show minutes before opening after he refused to cover five paintings depicting Jokowi.

f: Not-for-profit museum run by the UCCA Foundation, owned by Chinese and international patrons since 2017. 2025 partners: Louis Vuitton, Dior, Bloomberg and the Aranya seaside community; 901,435 visitors.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Beijing's culture bureau denied the permit for a 2019 Hung Liu show. UCCA pulled a Li Songsong painting in 2022 and the show closed early.

f: Run and paid for by the state-owned West Bund Group, per Pompidou's president. The Centre Pompidou partnership was renewed in 2023 for five years. Over 2 million visits.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Local officials had fewer than five works removed from the 2019 opening show, The Shape of Time. Pompidou says it does not self-censor.

f: Owned by the Government of Malaysia and run by the National Visual Art Development Board, a statutory body under the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture. Most exhibitions are free.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In February 2020 it removed four works from Ahmad Fuad Osman's retrospective. 55 collectors threatened to pull loans; a deputy minister asked for their return.

f: State museum funded by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism; entry is free. About 1.05 million visitors in 2016. German collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig gave 117 Western works.
w: Opened 1963 with over 110,000 works. A larger Jean Nouvel building was announced in 2014; no budget for either was found.

f: Run by the state-owned Power Station of Art; budget undisclosed and paid mainly from Shanghai city government funds. 2025 partners: Aesop, Denza, Langham hotels and lighting maker Flos.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Officials had Ai Weiwei's works and name removed from a 2014 show at its venue, the Power Station. Golshiri says a 2012 work was refused.

f: Opened 2024 by philanthropist Marisa Chearavanont through her organisation Khao Yai Art; no sponsors are named. Her husband Soopakij chairs CP Group, Thailand's largest private company.
w: Name to know: CP Group's CP Foods faced 2014 claims of slave-manned boats in its prawn-feed chain, then a 2015 US suit it called meritless.

f: Founded by collector and karaoke-club owner Qiao Zhibing, who told The Art Newspaper he paid for it. The state-owned West Bund Group invited him and built the surrounding park.
w: Opened 23 March 2019 in five former aviation fuel tanks. Time Out says Qiao invested with West Bund Group; no budget was found.

f: Founding sponsor Eczacıbaşı; main sponsor Doğuş Group with Bilgili Holding. The September 2026 sponsor panel lists Volvo, Visa, Mercedes-Benz, Nescafe, Paribu, TAV Airports and the Istanbul municipality.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A December 2023 sit-in delivered over 5,500 signatures for full-day free entry and open data. Eight artists and a collective pulled works in 2011.

f: State-owned foundation; 2024 income NOK 1,059M, gifts NOK 12.5M. Fredriksen Family Art Company lends its collection on a ten-year deal and funds four PhDs. AKO Foundation and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB give.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. A June 2022 appeal with over 100 signatures sought to end the Fredriksen deal. The family's wealth is tankers, drilling rigs and LNG ships.

f: Run by İKSV. Koç Holding is main sponsor for 2007 to 2036. Koç owns oil refiner Tüpraş and defence vehicle maker Otokar.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Arms and defence, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. Direnal-Istanbul protested Koç's sponsorship of the 2009 edition. The 2025 edition drew over 600,000 visitors.

f: Corporate museum of Borusan Holding, run by the Borusan Kocabıyık Foundation in the holding's headquarters. Group units: EnBW wind power, steel pipe, Caterpillar dealing, car sales. No outside sponsors.
w: Opened in 2011 during the 12th Istanbul Biennial. Borusan EnBW Enerji runs 725 MW of renewable plants.

f: Non-profit Serendipity Arts Foundation, founded by Hero Enterprise chair Sunil Kant Munjal. 2025 partners include the Goa government, Hero Insurance Broking, Hero Realty, Campa, Milton and foreign cultural institutes.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In December 2019 the festival sealed CAA and NRC artworks, citing a technical glitch. Police arrested four Dastaan musicians at the festival.

n: Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Mumbai City Museum
f: Public-private partnership of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, the Jamnalal Bajaj Foundation and INTACH. The Corporation paid INR 2.8 crore for the 2025 reopening repairs. No corporate sponsor named.
w: Mumbai's oldest museum, reopened in January 2025. Its expansion plan includes a Mumbai Modern Gallery.

f: Private museum of the Art & Photography Foundation. Founder Abhishek Poddar gave the collection and his family the land. Building donors include Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, Sunil Munjal, Citi and Tata.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2016 artists held a sit-in and a 1,000-signature petition against a state deal giving its parent foundation the Venkatappa Art Gallery.

f: Private trust founded in 1986, funded entirely by the Bengal Group. Chairman Abul Khair Litu co-founded AB Bank. It runs a fine arts gallery, a music festival and publishing.
w: In July 2024 the Anti-Corruption Commission endorsed a charge sheet against chairman Abul Khair Litu.

f: Non-profit company limited by guarantee. Its 2026 disclosure lists COMO Museum of Art, Khurram Kasim Art Foundation, HUM TV, HBL Art Committee, Kadist, AFIELD and private collectors.
w: Runs residencies and exhibitions in Karachi; over 500 artists have taken part in 25 years.

f: Autonomous body funded by the Union Ministry of Culture, founded in 1954. It runs the National Exhibition, the Triennale-India and seven regional centres. No sponsors are listed.
w: The government took over its management in April 2015, citing irregularities. A 2017 court petition alleged misappropriation of funds.

n: Anadolu Kültür (Depo and Diyarbakır Arts Center)
f: Founded 2002; runs Depo in Istanbul and the Diyarbakır Arts Center. Supporters named: Sigrid Rausing Trust, Civil Rights Defenders, Foundation for Arts Initiatives and Stiftung Mercator. No state money listed.
w: Chair Osman Kavala has been jailed since 2017 and got a life sentence in 2022. Turkey neither funds nor controls the group.

f: The Government of Sindh owns the palace, bought by the federal government after 1980. A board of trustees oversees it, and entry costs Rs 30. No sponsors are named.
w: Opened in September 1999 with Treasures of the Talpurs; it has since held over 20 exhibitions.

f: Statutory body under the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, founded in 1974, governed by a minister-led Executive Council. It runs district branches, scholarships and the National Art Gallery. No sponsors listed.
w: The venue for most Dhaka Art Summit editions, which the Samdani foundation produces.

f: Private non-profit founded in 2015 by collector and film producer Hamidreza Pejman, who bought the Argo Factory brewery in 2016. No government money paid for restoration; sponsors have since left.
w: Argo Factory has been closed since the war that began on 28 February 2026. Pejman says authorities shut its film series on a permit pretext.

f: State museum under the arts deputy of Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, which OFAC lists under its Iran program. The state set a 16.5 billion toman renovation budget.
w: Flags: Sanctions, State censorship or punishment. Western works stayed in the vault from 1979 to 1999. In 2017 the culture minister cancelled its Berlin and Rome loan show.

f: Government of India. A subordinate office of the Ministry of Culture, founded in 1954, with branches in Mumbai and Bengaluru. No corporate sponsor is named on its site.
w: At a February 2019 Mumbai opening, NGMA staff cut off Amol Palekar as he criticised the ministry over its advisory committees.
